articles.title_orig: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue.
The Trump administration on Monday announced it was tightening a loophole that has allowed Chinese tech firms to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing the most advanced A.I. chips through third countries.
The move comes just days ahead of President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in the wake of Nvidia, the creator of the most advanced AI chips, becoming enmeshed in an international scandal that prompted the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang and a fresh round of scrutiny over the company’s ties to China.
The new rule released by the Commerce Department will require that buyers of advanced semiconductors from certain countries will need to secure a license to sell or transfer those chips.The administration said the rule would specifically impact buyers from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, describing those countries as having a “higher than normal” risk of evading current sanctions.
The measure is set to go into effect in 90 days.
China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia. Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports.
The new rule will also give Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wide discretion as to which chips may require more safeguards. According to the rules, the secretary may inform a company selling AI chips “orally” about stricter export rules on certain items if the department believes there is “an unacceptable risk.”
The rules came days after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Lutnick for failing to properly oversee the chip exports to China in a CNBC interview on Sunday.
The rare public criticism came after Huang’s resignation as head of Nvidia in the wake of revelations about his extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected by the Commerce Department of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls, but a month-long investigation by the Commerce Department into Megaspeed was halted last year after a top Nvidia official intervened , according to the New York Times.
“Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said on CNBC on Sunday. “But Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
“President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage,” Bessent added.
Both Lutnick and Bessent are expected to travel with Trump to China this week, according to Semafor. Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Aside from AI chips, the first-of-its-kind summit will also focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons.
The federal government began restricting China's access to AI chips in Trump's first term, as both countries raced to become the leader  in this fast-evolving technology. The Biden administration intensified this policy , making the export of advanced chips to China illegal in 2022. Beijing nevertheless still succeeded in stockpiling thousands of chips to build its own AI systems thanks to an international smuggling network.
Last year, Trump reversed his own administration’s export restrictions, allowing Nvidia to sell two types of computer chip used in the development of artificial intelligence to "approved customers" in China in exchange for a portion of the revenue cut. Those moves are poised to draw more scrutiny next year when Democrats take control of Congress, with both chambers likely probing the Trump Administration's AI policies in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Congressional lawmakers have asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as a part of the investigation.

articles.title_orig: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.title_zh: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com .
Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.
Chase Bank's services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."
Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."
Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.
Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.
Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today."
U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.
A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.
Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.
"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.
The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal . (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a " widespread system outage " it had been dealing with that afternoon.)
Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.
"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."
He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.
"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.
When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.
"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."
Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down.
"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," she said in a statement to CBS News.
She also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.
"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.
She also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.
Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale.
Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."
"These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer."
Edited by Alain  Sherter and Aimee  Picchi
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: XBOX Black Friday Sale Starts November 19 with Our Biggest Sale of the Year on Games, Accessories and More!
articles.title_zh: XBOX Black Friday Sale Starts November 19 with Our Biggest Sale of the Year on Games, Accessories and More!
articles.content_orig:
By ELMIRA TANATAROVA, ASSISTANT LIFESTYLE EDITOR
Updated: 01:00 EST, 14 November 2026
Daily Mail journalists select and curate the products that feature on our site. If you make a purchase via links on this page we will earn commission - learn more
They're light, zippy and easy to store so it’s no surprise that cordless vacuum cleaners have become an indispensable addition to our cleaning arsenal.
All the big names, including Dyson, Shark – and even old faithful Henry – offer sleek stick cleaners boasting high-tech suction power and robust brush heads to rival traditional corded models. But in a crowded market, which of these nifty, handheld cleaners really deliver the best results?
To find out which are up to the job – and which are simply not – the Daily Mail Test Lab team put eight of the most popular models to the test, enlisting the help of leading home expert Lynsey Crombie. Known as the Queen of Clean to her hundreds of thousands of Instagram followers, Lynsey has two decades of professional cleaning experience and regularly shares her tips on ITV’s This Morning.
With prices ranging from £239 (and well under £200 in the Black Friday sale) to upwards of £600, the quest was on to discover which models are worth the spend and which simply don’t justify the price tag.
Lynsey Crombie, known as the Queen of Clean on Instagram, is one of the UK’s leading home experts.
A familiar face on This Morning and Good Morning Britain, she is trusted for her practical advice and simple, time-saving solutions.
With over 18 years of professional cleaning experience, Lynsey was the first cleaning influencer on Instagram.
Lynsey is also the author of four Sunday Times bestselling books, including her latest, The 15-Minute Clean, available on Amazon.
The cordless cleaners were put through their paces in a barrage of tests devised to assess how well they’d cope with different kinds of dust and debris on a range of flooring.
First, we challenged each cordless vacuum cleaner to pick up 20g of dirt, made up of flour, sand, oats and rice to mimic fine and coarse dust, from 2m samples of short pile and long pile carpet provided by Right Flooring London in Chiswick.
Then we repeated the same test on a strip of wood effect vinyl, supplied by Factory Direct Flooring, to see how they fared on hard flooring.
Next, we worked in 5g of pet hair, donated from clippings collected by Lola’s Pet Salon in north-west London, counting the number of passes it took to get rid of it.
Lynsey also conducted a corner test, scattering the dust mix in those awkward to reach nooks and crannies to see how well the stick cleaners would cope.
Then she carried each model up and down the stairs to gauge how easy or strenuous it would be to do this regularly in the home.
Each model was marked out of 5 for each test. But to come up with the final score, Test Lab analysed other key factors including run time, noise levels, number of attachments and how easy they were to empty and clean. Other metrics assessed across all models included how quickly the battery took to charge from empty to full – and of course, price.
In short, no stone was left unturned. We then picked our winners and ranked the cordless vacuum cleaners into three categories: standout buys, middle of the road models – and don’t buy disappointments.
No brand paid for promotion or influenced our verdicts in any way. Read more on why you can trust Daily Mail Test Lab's verdicts . We tell you how it REALLY is!
Write to Daily Mail Test Lab at testlab@dailymail.com with YOUR product review wish list.
Tough on dirt, our winners boasted the most impressive suction power and manoeuvrability as well as the best value for money. It turns out there's good reason Daily Mail readers tell us they're big fans of Shark's vacuums – not one, but TWO of its models topped our test rankings. In third place – and awarded best budget buy for its lower RRP – was the Gtech AirRAM2 . What about those Dysons? Read on to find out just how poorly they performed...
Full review: White and futuristic looking, with the touch of a Star Wars droid about it, the Shark PowerPro effortlessly tackled even the muckiest of floors. It beat the more expensive cleaners hands down making it excellent value for money. Its winning formula? Strong suction power combined with a seamless swivel action, which meant it performed well on both short and long pile carpet, sucking up dirt on the first pass without coughing up flour and rice at the sides like many of the other models.
The machine boasts what the brand describes as ‘FloorDetect’ technology, which means it senses floor type and adjusts the brush roll speed and suction power accordingly. And in our tests, this worked well.
Our expert Lynsey was also impressed by how easy it was to manoeuvre. ‘It feels like it does the moving for you rather than you using two hands and really pushing,’ she said, pointing out that the swivel head is so effective it requires very little wrist action, especially when tackling corners.
Lynsey Crombie, known as the 'Queen of Clean', came to the Daily Mail's Test Lab to help rate cordless vacuums
It wasn’t deterred by hard flooring either, sucking up the dust mix with a satisfying crunch.
When it came to the pet hair test, the Shark PowerPro made it look super easy, working effortlessly across all surfaces. Even if it didn’t get it all on the first stroke, it thoroughly cleaned up the rest on the second and third.
As one of the heavier models at 3.45kg, it was more of an effort to lug it up and down stairs. But there is a way to make it more compact – it folds in half, a clever feature which makes it easier to transport and store.
The PowerPro was also incredibly easy to clean. The dustbin canister, a generous 0.7 litres, opened at the touch of a button.
The only real downside? It’s quite noisy, so might not be suitable if you have nervous pets or need to keep a quiet household.
However, with a battery life of 50 minutes on eco mode (albeit, with a longer charge time of 3.5 hours) and a competitive price, this model – the cheaper of the two Sharks on test – was our clear overall winner.
On Amazon it has a customer review score of 4.4 out of five – with 72 per cent five-star reviews. One customer said it could clean their whole house on a single charge.
Lynsey said: ‘The PowerPro ticks all the boxes, and the biggest box it ticks is price. I'm thoroughly impressed with it for performance and value for money. A fantastic cordless vacuum!’
Full review: At first glance, the Gtech, which has a fixed head that doesn’t swivel, seemed bulkier and less versatile than other contenders. And yet in action, it moved easily, effortlessly gliding along the carpet sucking up everything in its wake. The cheapest model in our test, the rectangular brush head proved to be very effective, and you could hear it eating away at the dirt and pet hair, even if it did need three or four passes to pick everything up.
Smooth: Lynsey was impressed with the Gtech vacuum
The lack of rotation was a downside and should in theory have put it at a disadvantage when it came to corners. However, it worked better than expected, outdoing many more swivel-headed models. Because it fit so snugly against the wall, it made up for the lack of movement by sucking up dirt right up to the edges.
Lynsey was particularly impressed by its performance on long pile carpet. 'If you've got thick carpet, this is the one,’ said Lynsey, who found it made light work of the dust mix and pet hair.
However, it was less effective on the short pile carpet. ‘It more or less broke the hair down but left traces so I had to go over it more than once,’ she said. ‘And on the hard floor, it didn't pick everything up and took a couple of goes.’
On the plus side, it was easy to clean – you simply pulled out the canister from the brush head and emptied it. There is even a special attachment to make scraping the finer dust out easier.
Amazon reviewers give it 4.6 out of five.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.content_orig:
President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.
For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.
The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.
The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Slides 1.5% as Nvidia Drama Continues to Unfold — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Slides 1.5% as Nvidia Drama Continues to Unfold — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia ( NVDA -4.12% ) . On Friday, a day after Huang resigned as CEO, Musk posted on X that a petition to reinstate him was underway and that he was signing it.
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. ( SPCX -1.26% ) is building its AI data centers exclusively on Nvidia chips, and Nvidia holds a roughly $17 billion stake in SpaceX, so Musk has real skin in the game here.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/16/26
Huang was pushed out on Nov. 12 after Nvidia's board opened an investigation into reports that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort as part of one of now three alleged extramarital affairs. The board named Nvidia CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO as it begins a critical search for a permanent chief executive to replace Huang.
But now, a petition signed by nearly 200,000 people, including CEOs like Musk, Tim Sweeney of Epic Games and Tobias Lütke of Shopify ( SHOP +0.49% ) , is demanding that the board "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts." At the same time, a Financial Times report claims that Huang has been discussing such a return, though just hours ago, CNBC reported a source has told the news outlet that the board isn't considering a return at all.
The financial ties between SpaceX and Nvidia run both ways: Nvidia owns 122.8 million SpaceX shares , worth about $17 billion today, while SpaceX is a major customer -- Musk said in September that its two Colossus data centers in Memphis were running about 780,000 Nvidia chips, with hundreds of thousands more due by the end of the year. Musk said on SpaceX's second-quarter earnings call in August that he expects a "significant allocation" of Vera Rubin GPUs -- Nvidia's newest and most advanced chips -- next year.
Colette Kress is widely expected to rein in the industrywide financing Nvidia has been handing out, especially to neoclouds -- the upstart data center companies that buy Nvidia chips, install them in (often) leased data centers, and rent them out. If that spigot tightens, the consequences for SpaceX may actually be positive.
Image source: Getty Images.
The company ended Q3 with about $89.9 billion in cash and marketable securities, and has the ability to access traditional financing in a way that some neoclouds cannot, and if Nvidia starts rationing GPUs toward buyers who can actually pay upfront, SpaceX shouldn't have a problem being one of them. That means that the field of competition could narrow, keeping demand for SpaceX's compute high.
That said, SpaceX's AI unit's biggest customer is the AI model builder Anthropic, set to go public later this week . Anthropic depends in part on Neoclouds for the compute capacity it needs to deliver the growth investors expect. Anthropic's own filing warns that if partner financing dries up, contracted capacity could be delayed, repriced, or cut. Though it would likely increase Anthropic's reliance on SpaceX, it wouldn't have the capacity to spare in the short to medium term, and that could put Anthropic in a tough spot financially.

articles.title_orig: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.title_zh: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.content_orig:
Planes grounded. Office work ground to a halt.
The past few days have served as a vivid reminder of our deep and mostly unthinking dependence on technology. It’s powerful, it’s ubiquitous and yet, at times, it can be alarmingly fragile.
Old technology and new technology were the culprits. Starting on Thursday, Microsoft’s email, office and meeting software — delivered over the internet — stopped working for millions of users worldwide. Those cloud services were restored on Saturday.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights grounded after some of its aged data-handling equipment faltered, raising potential safety issues. The order was lifted Friday night, but hundreds of thousands of passengers were stranded over the weekend.
A telling irony is that both meltdowns were caused by attempted “upgrades” that went awry. New cables in the case of the F.A.A., and a planned increase in computing capacity in Microsoft’s case.
The upgrade challenge underlines the extraordinary complexity of multilayered combinations of hardware and software in major computing systems. Upset the delicate balance by making changes, even in an effort to improve performance, and you risk a system crash.
That happens frequently, though widespread outages are uncommon. The last big one came two years ago, when what should have been a routine software update by a security company, CrowdStrike, crashed millions of computers around the world that were running Microsoft Windows. Airlines grounded flights. Subways stopped. Operators of 911 lines couldn’t dispatch help. Stores shut down. Hospitals canceled surgeries. It took days to restore all the impaired machines.

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access. Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls more than 2%, extending slide to third day as Nvidia drags down AI trade
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders reacted to more developments surrounding Nvidia .
The Nasdaq Composite declined 2.49% to end at 24,509.76, while the S&P 500 dropped 1.92% to 7,416.59. Both indexes slid for the third straight session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 739.38 points, or 1.41%, closing at 51,608.17.
Shares of Nvidia were down 4.1%. The pressure came as a source familiar with the matter told CNBC that the chipmaker's board of directors is not discussing bringing back Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
Adding to the pressure, the Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent Nvidia's computing power located in other countries. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend also called for a " dramatic shakeup " at the company, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
"Two weeks ago investing in this name looked like a safe journey down a well-lit long hallway," said Mike Mussio, chief investment officer at FBB Capital Partners. Now, he added, "there are several dark corners that people feel they need to peek around to glean additional information before moving forward."
"There is plenty to digest, and many jumpy investors seem unwilling to stick around for answers," Mussio continued.
The embattled chipmaker is preparing to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped about 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"Strong results won't resolve the questions surrounding Jensen's departure," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations. Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology and Intel lost more than 7%, while Advanced Micro Devices declined 5%. Memory chip name Sandisk pulled back about 8%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined almost 7%, while software stock Oracle moved down about 5%.
The sell-off broadened beyond just AI-linked names as the session went on, with selling pressure picking up in areas like financials. In that group, Morgan Stanley , Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase shed more than 2%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering . The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.49% to end at 24,509.76, and the S&P 500 lost 1.92% to settle at 7,416.59. It was the third consecutive losing day for both indexes.
The Dow Industrials declined 739.38 points, or 1.41%, to 51,608.17.
Michael Burry of "Big Short" fame is retaining his bearish bets on Nvidia ahead of Tuesday's earnings, as well as those on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF , insurance company MetLife and military technology firm Palantir , according to a Monday blog post.
He said he has a "large position" in put options linked to those asset.
Burry closed out of puts in other parts of the equities market, including one hyperscaler that is central to the future of the super intelligence buildout, on volatility concerns.
"I closed out of the Oracle ( ORCL ) puts, and I also closed out of the last bit of my Caterpillar( CAT ) puts on the continued downward volatility in those names," he said.
The VIX volatility index, a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, jumped as much as 25% Monday to a session high of 24.05.
That left the VIX at the highest in a week, since it reached 25.08 on Nov. 9, and was the largest percentage gain since the VIX soared almost 60% on Nov. 5.
The VIX is now on track to rise for a third consecutive day for the firs time since Nov. 2.
The S&P 500 was down nearly 2% on Monday, and all sectors linked to the index except for one suffered losses.
The consumer staples sector was higher by 0.3% in afternoon trading. Conversely, every other S&P 500 sector fell, with information technology and communication services taking the lead on that front. Those two were down 2.7% and 2.6%, respectively.
Consumer discretionary and energy were also key laggards, with the former falling 2.2% and the latter down 2%.
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on a investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, the person said. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or Nvidia secrets.
Read the full story here .
— Seema Mody and Kif Leswing
Northcoast Research downgraded Costco Wholesale to neutral from buy on Monday after the stock's run higher this year.
The wholesale club has shown "remarkable success" as inflation drove shoppers into its stores, analyst Chuck Cerankosky said. However, shares currently trade at 48.4 times earnings.
"At multiples comparable to those of tech stocks and the rate at which the company is growing earnings, we believe shares of Costco Wholesale are valued fairly," he wrote in a note to clients.
The stock, which has gained 29% year to date, hit a 52-week high on Monday.
Despite uncertainty about the future of chipmaker Nvidia's leadership, there's strength ahead for semiconductors, according to Trivariate Research.
The firm expects "strong" earnings results from Nvidia this week and from memory maker Micron next month, supporting positive trends in returns over the next year.
"We think Semiconductors have a reasonable chance of being 50% higher in a year," Adam Parker at Trivariate wrote in a Sunday analysis.
Shares of Nvidia bounced on Thursday but failed to build on that progress on Friday, leading analysts at Wolfe to reconsider the $150 support level maintained last week.
"The stock successfully held that key $150 support level, after Thursday's notable intraday reversal. Unfortunately, the stock failed to build off of that reversal on Friday. Should price end up losing it, the next major support level sits around $100," Rob Ginsberg at Wolfe wrote in a Sunday note.
Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite.
The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level.
Read the full story here .
The three major averages kicked off the first trading session of the week in the red.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 declined 0.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 78 points, or 0.2%.
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive technology being exported to China .
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department, in a press release, said that the BIS rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." Read more .

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.content_orig:
California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta's office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT "misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public."
Bonta's office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was "entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI's choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight."
OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab."
He said the company has "undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity" since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a "framework for additional identification and disclosure" of unintended activity, and will "continue to engage" with Bonta's office "to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a "warning shot" and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents.
Bonta's office said the company's "disregard for the public safety" created a "public nuisance" in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in "unfair" or "fraudulent" practices.
"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," Bonta said.
The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined.
The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections.
The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society.
OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company's website that its "first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity" and in a way that empowers "people broadly," not just a concentrated few.
"We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem," they wrote. They went on to say that "AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions."
They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. "The goal wasn't to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use," they wrote.
The company called the Hugging Face attack "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed."
Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta's office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks "may just be the tip of the iceberg," but the scope of the problem isn't fully known because OpenAI hasn't answered "detailed questions" about them.
In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure.
Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors .
Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release.
"This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated," OpenAI said in a statement.
Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should "pass off the blame to machines" while letting those who create them escape accountability.
"The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions," Bonta said at a news conference Monday.
"Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards," he said.
Bonta's office said it is encouraging "anyone with information relevant to this case" to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report .
He said his office is also watching other AI companies "closely," but declined to elaborate.

articles.title_orig: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.title_zh: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.content_orig:
Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government.
The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the mass trial , saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions.
A lawyer for several of the defendants, speaking on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients.
When asked about those claims, the Bahraini government said in a statement that all of the defendants had been “afforded their full legal rights and safeguards, including the right of defense,” and that complaints of mistreatment would be referred for investigation.
“This case was about criminal conduct, not faith or belief,” the government added.
The Bahraini authorities had accused the defendants of forming a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. According to a statement from the Bahraini public prosecution department, published by the state news agency, the defendants had worked to undermine the Bahraini government, and the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials.
“They had also sought to change the system of government by force and unlawful means through incitement to commit terrorist acts, acts of rioting and sabotage,” the statement added.

articles.title_orig: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.title_zh: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing calls from lawmakers for an investigation following a report that alleged that a member of his staff provided information to police against Arab citizens in an attempt to influence last month’s elections. The claims, which Netanyahu’s office denies, were made on an Israeli TV news show this weekend.
The controversy centers on the widely publicized arrest of three activists from the Arab party Raam in southern Israel early on the morning of the October 27 election over an alleged cash-for-votes scheme. Throughout the day, Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly amplified the arrests to mobilize their own voters, alleging Raam was trying to “steal the elections.”
Courts later rejected police requests to keep the suspects in custody, saying that the arrests were carried out without a valid search or arrest warrant. All suspects have since then been released.
According to an investigation by Channel 12’s “Uvda,” the allegation originated in Netanyahu’s office. The day before the elections, the report alleges, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, bypassed standard reporting channels and personally contacted the police commissioner to alert him about the activists, passing on information.
Norden allegedly referred police to a separate source who was said to hold information about the activists. But the source was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the report said.
Based on Norden’s complaint and the information provided by the former employee, police carried out the arrests on election day, the report alleged.
On Monday evening, Israel’s Attorney General said she would hold a discussion on the transfer of information from the Prime Minister’s Office to the police. “As part of the discussion, all aspects relating to the matter will be examined,” the Attorney General’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s office strongly denied the Channel 12 report, saying it was “false and grounds for libel,” but confirmed that Nordan had passed information to the police.
“Criminal information reached Chief of Staff Ido Norden, he fulfilled his duty as expected of any law-abiding citizen and connected that person to the police,” his office said in a statement Sunday evening. Norden learned on the morning of the elections that a person “was indeed caught with tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Raam slips,” the statement continued, referring to a suspect who had already been released.
In a statement, Israel Police said it would examine “the decision-making processes, the chain of reporting, the working interfaces between the relevant police units, and the division of responsibility” related to the allegations in the Channel 12 report. “All police actions, including the operation carried out on election morning, were taken out of commitment and transparency toward the public, and with the aim of protecting the integrity of the elections,” police said.
On Monday evening, the Attorney General requested a pause in this examination until there is a decision “on the appropriate format for the inquiry.”
The main opposition party is calling for an immediate investigation. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the conduct of Netanyahu and his circle is “a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” warning that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, there will be no more fair and proper elections in Israel.”
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
Two Arab parties that saw record voter turnout in the elections also demanded an immediate criminal investigation.
“The arrest of our activists in the Negev on the morning of the elections and the attempt to silence Arab Knesset members, if proven, is a direct attack on the integrity of the elections and the will of the voters,” Raam said in a statement, referring to Israel’s parliament. The Joint List called to establish an independent commission of inquiry – the state’s highest investigative body – and suspend all involved police and Shin Bet officials.
“Netanyahu tried to steal our vote, but our vote is what will bring him down. His place is not in the Prime Minister’s Office, but in the interrogation room and before the court,” the party said in a statement.
Since losing his parliamentary majority in the October 27 vote, Netanyahu and his allies have raised various allegations against the Arab parties, accusing them of bribery, foreign funding, and fraud. David Zini, the director of the Shin Bet domestic security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, has pressed to investigate Arab politicians over allegations of foreign interference, but so far hasn’t presented any public evidence to support the allegations against them. According to the Channel 12 report, Zini demanded to wiretap five Arab lawmakers before election day.
The request was refused at the last minute by the attorney general because he did not present any evidence to back his request, Channel 12 reported.
In a statement, the Shin Bet said it carried out “various activities in accordance with its powers under the law.”
Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and the interim chair of the crucial Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said on Monday that he would summon the Shin Bet and police chiefs to discuss alleged foreign interference attempts in the election.

articles.title_orig: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.title_zh: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: U.S. loses measles-elimination status, erasing decades of progress
LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that it’s time to admit that Brexit has not delivered for the U.K. and that the country needs a much closer relationship with the European Union to combat growing isolationism around the world.
He compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum , to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes,” in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked .
“Well, I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said in a speech on foreign policy at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London’s financial district. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained .”
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the U.K. was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move toward more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It was exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham spoke ahead of a U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on Friday that is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc, a decade after the U.K.’s vote to leave and six years after the departure in 2020.
It is expected to seal a trade deal for food and drink , agreements on energy and emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham argued that the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries is down sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4% to 8% of the U.K.’s gross domestic product, he said.
Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy , but U.K. politicians have been wary of reopening a painful debate.
Not Burnham. He said that soon after the summit, he will open a national conversation on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc. His spokesman Tom Wells said Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome .”
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as center-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country : The referendum vote was 52% in favor of leaving the EU and 48% in support of staying in.
Brexit-backing former Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson said if Burnham tried to take Britain back into the EU , “people will wake up to what is going on. They won’t want it, and he won’t succeed.”

articles.title_orig: A Bull Market for Pokémon Cards, Fueled by Pikachu and Nostalgia
articles.title_zh: A Bull Market for Pokémon Cards, Fueled by Pikachu and Nostalgia
articles.content_orig:
Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection is officially back in stock at Amazon ahead of the retailer's massive Black Friday sale , which kicks off on November 19.
We've seen fleeting appearances of this elusive UPC at other retailers recently, but this is the first time we've spotted anything resembling consistent availability at a major retailer.
The catch? It's $399.99. Yeah, that's pricey.
Unfortunately, it's also not too far removed from the going rate for the Night variant on the secondary market. TCGplayer currently lists it at a median price of around $399.99, although its market price is closer to $372.64, with the most recent sale coming in at $371.87.
So, Amazon is charging a little more than the current market rate, but we're still talking about a price that's dramatically higher than the original MSRP.
If you are looking to pick one up on the secondary market, Amazon is certainly a reliable, yet expensive option for buying a guaranteed new box, and TCGplayer is a slighty less expensive option if you'd prefer to buy at a trusted resale site.
Just to note as well, if you do opt for purchasing the Amazon listing "sold and shipped by Amazon.com", not by any third-party reseller.
Originally released on November 6, the Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection retails for $179.99. If you've never encountered a UPC before, think of these as the ultimate collector's boxes, packed with exclusive cards, premium accessories, and plenty of booster packs.
For the 30th Anniversary, collectors can choose between two variants: the Day box, featuring Espeon ex, and the Night box, featuring Umbreon ex. Both celebrate the TCG's past, present, and future with premium storage, game accessories, and exclusive promo artwork.
Each collection comes with some gorgeous cards, including a few of my personal favourites featuring artwork by YOSHIROTTEN. You'll find a foil Pikachu ex promo in either a Day or Night design, alongside an Espeon ex promo in the Day Edition or an Umbreon ex promo in the Night Edition.
It doesn't stop there. Each box also includes a themed playmat featuring Pikachu, Espeon, or Umbreon, 65 matching card sleeves, a heavy-duty deck box, a metal flip coin featuring Espeon or Umbreon, and a metal damage counter die.
The biggest draw, though, is the 29 Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration booster packs, alongside a Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Classic Collection booster pack containing three etched reprint cards. You'll also get a code card for Pokémon TCG Live.
Robert Anderson is a Senior Commerce Editor for IGN. Based in London, UK, he is a qualified journalist with a Bachelor of Arts in Journalism (First Class Degree) and over seven years of professional writing and editing experience.
You can usually find Robert lost in open-world RPG games like Elden Ring and Cyberpunk 2077. Outside of gaming, his passions include reading comics (especially Superman, Batman, and Spider-Man), taking photos, and keeping up with the latest in film and TV.
His primary coverage focuses on tracking down the best gaming deals and diving into the fast-paced world of Trading Card Games (TCGs). He regularly covers everything from the latest releases in Pokémon TCG and the most expensive cards to comprehensive Magic: The Gathering buying guides .

articles.title_orig: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.title_zh: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.
Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.
Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.
The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.
The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.
But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase says bank transactions are back to normal after outage online and at some branches
Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally Monday evening after a nationwide outage that had some customers reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
“Transactions are now posting normally,” a Chase spokesperson said around 6:30 p.m.
The outage began Monday morning, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Chase said at around 4 p.m. on X that “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware system” and that it was working to resolve it.
The issues had been affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
The issue was not “cyber-related,” the bank said, and did not  impact the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
The bank said that customers still had access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal.
Regulators were in touch with the big banks affected “immediately,” a person familiar with the situation said earlier Monday. They “quickly determined this was contained and service was already in process of restoration,” the person said then.
The issues at Chase were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
By late afternoon Monday, several Chase bank branches in Manhattan appeared to be operating normally. Customers leaving a branch at 6th Avenue and W. 51st Street told NBC News they didn’t know there had been a problem until they arrived at the branch, where they were told by employees that they’d gotten there at just the right time.
“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues with Chase accounts also appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
A spokesperson for PNC Bank said it was “not experiencing any direct impact. We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving.”
Truist bank said its services “are operating normally,We continue to closely monitor our systems and are not aware of any broad service disruptions at this time.”
Customers at Wells Fargo also experienced delays, but the company did not provide a statement.
Citibank likewise declined to comment.
A spokesperson for Capital One said the bank “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time.”
— WMAQ’s Lauren Stauffer and Leigh Lesniak contributed reporting from Chicago.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
articles.content_orig:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.
Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.
This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.
This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.
The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.
For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" it was dealing with Monday afternoon, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop .
"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said Monday evening. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights." The outage lasted about 90 minutes.
Earlier, United said it was "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights."
A memo from the union representing United Airlines pilots indicated the issue was with the airline's weight and balance calculation system, noting: "The Company cannot provide outbound flights with final weights."
A United spokesperson said there's no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity issue.
The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 715 delayed flights late Monday afternoon, although it was unclear how many of those were the result of the short-lived tech issue. About an hour and a half after the outage was resolved, it didn't appear that the brief outage was having a major impact on the carrier's flights, with delays and cancellations roughly in line with its competitors.
The disruption for the Chicago-based carrier came less than 24 hours after the Federal Aviation Administration said airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal following Friday's hourslong ground stop.
The United computer problem was just the latest high-profile technology meltdown.
Earlier in the day, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every U.S. flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email services. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.
Kathryn  Krupnik and Kris  Van Cleave contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 10 Numbers That Might Change How You See Asia
articles.title_zh: 10 Numbers That Might Change How You See Asia
articles.content_orig:
President Trump’s trip to Asia this week will largely be seen as a test of American power in the main region where the United States and China compete for influence.
His meetings in Manila and Shenzhen, China, will be scrutinized for shifts on trade and security. Deals he might strike with Beijing — plus a gathering with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia — will put the world’s great-power contest on display, as all three seek to show strength.
But Asia is not just a theater of competition. Many countries in the region have become wealthier, more technologically advanced and increasingly interconnected . Especially now, as China’s military becomes more threatening and the United States less reliable, they are hedging against greatness and relying more on neighbors.
Asian students and workers are moving to neighboring states. Countries with expanding defense industries are selling weapons to new partners. Nations that compete for high-tech investment are even making plans to cooperate on energy and cybersecurity .
“They’re all looking at what more they can do together when the great powers are behaving so badly,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam and adjunct professor of geopolitics at Fulbright University in Ho Chi Minh City. “If you’re a middle power, you’re thinking ‘I need more options.’”
Here are a few numbers that provide a sense of what the region contributes to the global economy, and how its nations are becoming more bound together to shape the world.

articles.title_orig: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.title_zh: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.
